title: A quantum generative model for in silico clinical trials using scarce training datasets
authors: Olatz Sanz Larrarte, Reza Dastbasteh, Roberto Sanchez-Navarro, Maria Diez-Campelo, Felipe Prosper, Ana Alfonso-Pierola, Mikel Hernaez, Sara Capponi, Pedro Crespo Bofill, Josu Etxezarreta Martinez
abstract: In silico methods have emerged as a strategy to complement clinical trials. These are particularly relevant for rare or heterogeneous diseases for which traditional methods are costly or difficult to apply. While classical generative models have shown an extremely good ability to generate high fidelity data when trained using extensive databases, they often struggle when the available samples for training are scarce. In this work, we leverage the potential of quantum computers to represent complex probability distributions to generate high fidelity in silico patients. We propose a pipeline able to combine asymmetric databases into a quantum circuit that serves as a quantum generative model. We evaluate the efficacy of our proposal using a database of Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) patients with 7 clinical variables as a proof-of-concept. We executed our quantum generative model in the IBM Heron r2 ``ibm\_basquecountry'' superconducting quantum computer and compare our method with well known classical baselines. Our results show that the quantum generative model surpasses the classical generative models in generalization and expressivity metrics, indicating its potential validity to generate high fidelity in silico patients for clinical trials.
summary: This paper introduces a quantum generative model designed to create realistic synthetic patient data for rare diseases where real data is scarce. It leverages quantum circuits, trained on maximum entropy principles, to model complex probability distributions. Results show this quantum approach outperforms established classical generative models in fidelity and expressivity metrics.
main_problem: The core problem is generating high-fidelity synthetic patient data for *in silico* clinical trials, especially when training datasets are scarce due to rare or heterogeneous diseases.
main_result: The proposed quantum generative model surpasses classical generative models in both generalization and expressivity metrics, indicating its potential for generating high-fidelity patient data.
method: The authors propose a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline that maps the target joint probability distribution into a quantum circuit for sampling.
model_or_system: The model uses a quantum generative approach, encoding the joint probability distribution into a quantum state, compressing it via a Matrix Product State (MPS), and executing the resulting circuit on a superconducting quantum computer (IBM Heron r2).
key_observables: Generalization metrics include Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD); expressivity is measured by Random Forest classification accuracy, AUC, and Coverage Ratio.
important_parameters: The study tests performance across varying subsample sizes ($n_{	ext{selected}} \in \{100, 150, 200, 300, 400\}$) of the scarce data.
main_assumptions: The primary limitations are the current noise levels and limited qubit counts of quantum devices, necessitating error-detection and post-selection steps.
figures_summary: Figures compare MAE/JSD and Accuracy/AUC vs. sample size, showing the quantum model's consistent superiority over classical baselines. Figure 4 displays confusion matrices confirming the quantum model's difficulty in distinguishing real from synthetic samples.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of data scarcity in clinical trials, details the quantum generative pipeline (encoding via MPS, circuit mapping), compares performance against classical GANs/VAEs using multiple metrics, and concludes with empirical results demonstrating quantum superiority.
why_interesting: While the application is biomedical, the core methodology involves advanced quantum circuit design, state preparation (MPS), and benchmarking against classical ML models, which is highly relevant to quantum algorithm development for complex data distributions.

Figure 4: Row-normalized 2×2 confusion matrices of the Random Forest classifier for the pro- posed quantum model and classical baselines (aggregated GAN baseline obtained by averaging the row-normalized confusion matrices of CTGAN and CopulaGAN) across all sample sizes. Values close to 0.5 indicate near-random discrimination between real and synthetic samples, supporting higher indistinguishability.
